other-interests-4c9a9d57c5.headline: AI Chatbots Are Hardwired to Defend the Status Quo
other-interests-4c9a9d57c5.fulltext:
Summary:
A comprehensive study by researchers at the University of Waterloo reveals that large language models (LLMs) suffer from a pronounced “status quo bias,” consistently recommending existing, high-emission choices over innovative, climate-friendly alternatives. Evaluating 11 prominent AI models across nearly 55,000 tested prompts, the team found that chatbots endorsed existing policies twice as often as proposed climate reforms and recommended electric vehicles far below actual real-world adoption rates. The findings suggest that defaulting to generative AI for consumer and policy decisions poses an overlooked barrier to decarbonization.
Key Facts:
- The Policy Bias Gap: When asked to evaluate whether to proceed with an initiative, AI models approved existing, status-quo plans 70% of the time, but endorsed novel climate policies only 34% of the time.
- Lagging Behind Real-World Adoption: Across jurisdictions, AI platforms recommended electric vehicles at rates lower than existing national market sales, even in EV-dominant countries like Norway.
- Scale of Testing: Researchers tested 11 LLMs across more than 7,500 distinct queries spanning transit, home heating, diets, and public policy, yielding nearly 55,000 total benchmarked prompts.
Source: University of Waterloo
As millions of consumers, business leaders, and policymakers turn to conversational artificial intelligence for everyday purchasing advice and strategic planning, algorithms are quietly shaping societal decision-making. Yet because large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive historical corpora reflecting past human choices, their recommendations inevitably reflect entrenched historical norms.
In psychology, the tendency to prefer existing conditions over novel alternatives is known as the “status quo bias.”
Now, a pioneering computational and environmental study from the University of Waterloo demonstrates that this cognitive bias is deeply baked into the underlying architecture of commercial AI chatbots—with detrimental consequences for global climate goals.
The study, which evaluated 11 major LLMs across nearly 55,000 prompt iterations, represents the first systematic investigation into how generative AI status quo bias influences climate-related recommendations.
The results reveal that chatbots systematically steer users toward high-emission defaults in transportation, home energy, consumer habits, and public policy.
“I think it’s worth being aware that these models, even the new ones, have blind spots,” said lead researcher Seth Wynes, Ph.D., professor in the Faculty of Environment at the University of Waterloo. “It’s good for consumers to be aware of this bias and if you’re asking for advice on a topic, you could ask it to make the case for doing something new.”
Evaluating 55,000 Prompts Across 11 Language Models
To test whether AI chatbots passively preserve the status quo, the Waterloo research team developed a standardized library of more than 7,500 unique queries. The questions covered high-impact personal and civic domains where carbon trade-offs are significant:
- Vehicle acquisitions and personal transit choices
- Home heating systems and residential energy retrofits
- Dietary preferences and food recipes
- Regional and municipal climate policy decisions
Each query was tested across a battery of at least six distinct LLMs, producing an empirical dataset of nearly 55,000 model responses.
The bias was most pronounced in political and civic governance scenarios. When asked whether a government or organization should proceed with a plan, the language models approved the proposal 70% of the time if it was framed as an existing, active policy. However, when the exact same objective was presented as a novel climate intervention or regulatory change, the models agreed to proceed just 34% of the time.
Where climate trade-offs existed in policy deliberations, platforms reinforced decisions the user had already made with double the frequency of alternative paths.
Lagging Behind Real-World Clean Tech Transitions
The researchers found that while LLMs adapt somewhat to regional user contexts, their baseline advice still lags significantly behind actual real-world transitions.
For example, when a prompt indicated that the user was located in Norway, where battery-electric vehicles command the overwhelming majority of new car registrations, chatbots were more inclined to recommend an EV than if the user specified they were in Canada.
However, in both countries, the frequency with which AI recommended purchasing an electric vehicle fell substantially below the actual, verified rate at which EVs are being bought today in those markets.
“In almost every jurisdiction, the LLMs are working at a slower pace of change than is needed, so they recommend fewer EV models than what are actually being sold today,” Dr. Wynes explained. “It might be very good for AI to favour the status quo for lots of other things, such as proven medical advice, but climate is where we really do need change.”
Mitigating Algorithmic Inertia
The findings highlight a growing risk: as generative search engines and conversational chatbots become embedded into commercial purchasing flows and enterprise advisory workflows, their built-in bias toward historical habits could delay essential sustainability transitions.
While favoring the status quo may offer useful guardrails in safety-critical domains like established clinical medicine or structural engineering, applying that same inertia to rapidly evolving challenges like the energy transition actively impedes progress.
The research team plans to track future iterations of frontier models to evaluate whether updated fine-tuning approaches or integrated browsing tools mitigate this inertia, or if in-platform AI transactions will further cement legacy high-carbon consumption patterns.

Abstract
Large language models exhibit status quo bias in climate-relevant advice
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by consumers and decision-makers to provide advice, including on choices relevant to climate change.
Status quo bias is the tendency to favor existing conditions over change. It is well-documented in human psychology and could be problematic in LLM climate advice given that rapid societal changes are required to sufficiently reduce emissions.
We evaluated 7548 queries spanning multiple domains including vehicle purchases, recipes, home heating, and climate-relevant policy trade-offs. Each of these queries was tested on at least six different LLMs for a total of 54 888 prompts.
By asking climate-relevant trade-off questions that held all variables constant except status quo framing, we found that LLMs had, on average, 7.5 times higher odds of recommending a course of action when it was framed as preserving existing conditions than when it required change, a finding that persists in leading 2026 models.
In consumer contexts, LLMs were 4.1 times more likely to recommend electric vehicles to users who already owned one and vehicle recommendations correlated with regional adoption rates (rs = 0.48, p < .001) but rarely exceeded them. Recipe recommendations demonstrated no partiality for (low-emissions) plant-based options (40% vegetarian or vegan).
These consumer findings complement the evidence from the more controlled tradeoff findings and together suggest that, on balance, LLMs systematically favor existing conditions in their recommendations. While conservative advice may be appropriate in many contexts, climate mitigation requires departure from high-emission norms.
Users seeking climate-relevant advice from LLMs should be aware of this tendency, and developers of climate or consumer-oriented applications may wish to address it through system prompts.

india-deep-tech-28b8fd9843.fulltext:
Insider Brief
- Bengaluru-based Quanfluence has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Chiratae Ventures, with Pi Ventures and Rainmatter by Zerodha participating.
- The company plans to use the funding to build a full-stack photonic quantum computer combining its photonic chips, control electronics and software.
- Quanfluence is targeting early processors by 2027 and larger systems by 2029, building on its work in photonic integrated circuits, electronic circuits, quantum light generation and photonic devices.
PRESS RELEASE — Quanfluence, a Bengaluru-based deep technology company building photonic quantum computers, has raised USD 10 million in a funding round led by Chiratae Ventures. Pi Ventures, which led Quanfluence’s seed round in 2024, returned as co-investor. Rainmatter by Zerodha also invested in this round.
The capital will be deployed to build Quanfluence’s full-stack photonic quantum computer, bringing together indigenously designed photonic chips, control electronics and the software layer into a single system. The company has a roadmap with early processors by 2027 and larger scalable machines by 2029.
Since its previous funding round, Quanfluence has built out several of the core technologies required for its full-stack architecture. The company has designed and fabricated multiple photonic integrated circuits (PICs) and electronic integrated circuits (EICs), developed low-loss chip-to-fiber coupling designs, and demonstrated the generation of quantum light states. It has also made significant progress on photonic chips for light-matter interactions. In parallel, Quanfluence has moved parts of its technology beyond the laboratory: its photonic Ising machine has been productized, and several quantum devices developed by the company are now commercially available.
Sujoy Chakravarty, Co-founder and CEO, Quanfluence, said: “Our goal at Quanfluence has never been to build a better experiment. It has been to build a useful quantum computer. We chose photonics because we believe it gives us a path to scale. Over the last few years, we have built the core pieces: the ICs, the electronics, the optics and the algorithms. This funding allows us to bring those pieces together into a complete system.”
Started in 2021 by Sujoy Chakravarty, Ravi Mehta, Biman Chattopadhyay, Aditi Vaidya, Prof. Anil Prabhakar of IIT Madras and Prof. Sandeep Goyal of IISER Mohali, Quanfluence is incubated at the IIT Madras Incubation Cell. Three of its founders previously built Silicon and Beyond, a semiconductor IP company acquired by Synopsys. The team pairs that chip-design track record with expertise in quantum optics to develop its core technology in-house.
“As a fund, we are keen to back indigenous deeptech bets led by exceptional founders. Quantum Computing is at an inflection point and we believe photonics is amongst the most credible routes to a machine that scales outside the lab. What drew us to Quanfluence is a rare combination of a team that has already built and exited a semiconductor IP business, now applying that same engineering discipline to quantum optics,” shared Venkatesh Peddi, Managing Director & Partner, Chiratae Ventures.
“Since our initial investment in Quanfluence, we have seen the team make meaningful progress in translating their vision for a deeply complex technology into a credible path towards commercially relevant quantum computing. Building differentiated quantum hardware requires deep technical expertise, patient execution and the ability to attract world-class scientific and engineering talent, and Quanfluence has continued to demonstrate all three. Our follow-on investment reflects our growing conviction in the team, their technology, and the opportunity to build a globally significant quantum computing company from India.” Shubham Sandeep – Partner, Pi Ventures
“The global quantum computing landscape is at an inflection point, transitioning from academic curiosity to serious, industrial-scale development. For decades, India has been a massive consumer of deep technology built elsewhere; we are proud to partner with a team that is decisively shifting us to becoming creators of it. Building a universal quantum computer is an incredibly hard, highly ambitious mountain to climb. By taking a calculated risk on a highly differentiated photonic architecture, Quanfluence is carving out a completely unique path. What makes them stand out is their pragmatism. They are cleverly de-risking the massive long-term hardware challenge with near-term revenue streams, all while building a core piece of India’s sovereign quantum capability. This is a hardware-first, patent-backed bet on India’s deep-tech future, and we are glad to be doing our bit by supporting them.” Abhinav Singh Negi – Lead, Climate and Deeptech, Rainmatter by Zerodha.

work-careers-86030da9e0.headline: GCCs under pressure: Why some India centers are cutting jobs or closing
work-careers-86030da9e0.fulltext:
A string of layoffs and closures at India’s GCCs in recent months is highlighting a shift in the country’s GCC story, with parent-company restructuring, and AI-led productivity gains putting some centres under pressure even as India continues to attract new investments.
Recent exits include Cambium Networks, which shut its Bengaluru GCC in October, affecting around 200 employees, and Hy-Vee, which closed its India engineering centre in June, impacting around 150 employees.
According to Alouk Kumar, founder and CEO of Inductus Group, parent-company restructuring and global cost-cutting account for an estimated 50–60 per cent of layoffs in India’s GCCs. AI-led productivity and workforce redesign account for another 15–20 per cent, while GCC-specific portfolio weakness contributes 10–15 per cent. 5–10 per cent is linked to GCC closures or parent-company exits, with the remaining cases stemming from local restructuring, performance issues, acquisitions and other factors.
Gaurav Vasu, CEO and founder of UnearthInsight, echoed that key reasons include sector-specific challenges, as automotive, SaaS, and manufacturing face global weakness. More than 400 GCCs could remain under stress over the next few years.
AI is also shrinking traditional software development cycles and reducing the need for large developer teams, particularly in SaaS and software product GCCs, while driving global restructuring. Additionally, some GCCs face operational constraints as their mandates have changed from when they were set up 10-15 years ago.
“GCCs are tenured, and some may not live up to their full potential, still running like a back-office or support operation. If the leadership doesn’t view the India center as an IP creation or innovation center, there may be full-fledged shutdowns. The company may then take work back to a service provider, or to the headquarters,” he said.
Yajna Prakash, Partner & Executive Director, Acclime India noted that over 50 per cent of India’s GCCs are estimated to be sub-scale, with easily replaceable skills and limited ownership across engineering, product or P&L. AI is disrupting these centres, particularly the 1.1–1.3 million employees in repeatable roles.
“80 per cent of GCCs surveyed by EY reported that less than 10 per cent of their leadership roles are based in India. Our Ecosystem Dilemma research, based on structured interviews with GCC leaders across seven industry segments, found a similar pattern. India can design at a world-class level, but decision-making authority often remains with the parent organisation,” she said.
Layoffs
Kumar said GCCs saw 5,500–6,000 layoffs in 2025 even as they added around 150,000 jobs, with cuts largely driven by parent-company restructuring and portfolio recalibration rather than weakness in India’s GCC model. Industry estimates put 2026 layoffs at 4,000–5,000, again primarily due to parent-company restructuring.
Smaller GCCs are particularly vulnerable when they lack scale, have narrow mandates, limited technology adoption, few opportunities to diversify capabilities or struggle to attract talent.
Moreover, Prakash said, it is getting more expensive to run a GCC in India, particularly at the specialist end. GCC salaries are projected to rise 10.4 per cent in 2026, while GCC roles carry about a 20 per cent premium over equivalent non-GCC roles. AI, GenAI, and ML roles command skill premiums of up to 40 per cent.
“Attrition stands at 15–20 per cent, and 60 per cent of hiring now comes from other GCCs. Smaller centres are competing for the same scarce talent as larger centres with deeper pockets. India remains highly competitive on talent depth and speed to scale. What has changed is the idea that a GCC can justify its existence on labour cost alone,” she said.
However, smaller GCCs are not necessarily a bad proposition. Kumar noted that the future belongs to smaller but highly specialised GCCs.
“A 75-100 headcount centre specialising in AI/ML, cybersecurity or product engineering can be more valuable than a 500-person centre doing commoditised transaction processing. The new measure is not how many people a GCC employs, but what it owns,” he noted.
Strategic Scaling
Prashakth Kamath, Marketing Director & Head of Global Demand Generation at Straive, said the key question is how a GCC’s mandate is changing, with centres potentially shrinking in some areas while becoming more strategic in others.
“Scale provides advantages, but by itself does not guarantee relevance. A smaller GCC owning a critical product, platform, AI capability or specialised domain function can be important to the parent organisation. Equally, a much larger centre with a mandate concentrated around highly standardised or increasingly automatable work may face pressure to transform,” he said.
Jaikumar Subramanian, Partner and GCC Industry leader- Diversified Industries, Deloitte South Asia, said, “The GCC value proposition is evolving beyond cost efficiency. As demand grows for specialised talent, particularly in AI and advanced technologies, success will be measured by value created, innovation delivered, IP generated and the strategic importance of the mandate. AI will streamline repetitive processes while unlocking new opportunities across enterprise modernisation, customer experience, data-led decision-making and product innovation.”
He noted that operating models are likely to become more flexible, with captive, BOT, hybrid and outsourced structures continuing to coexist. Technology partners will remain integral to the ecosystem, supporting capabilities across cloud, cybersecurity, engineering, managed services and AI transformation. Importantly, changes in ownership or delivery models do not necessarily imply a shift of work away from India. The next generation of leading GCCs will be defined by their ability to combine specialised capabilities, technology, productivity and ecosystem partnerships to secure increasingly strategic global mandates.
Transformation
Experts expect India’s GCC landscape to polarise between 2026 and 2030, with large, strategic multi-function centres and small, specialised, AI-native GCCs gaining ground. Kumar noted that large GCCs may account for 40 per cent of new mandates and specialised centres for 60 per cent, while smaller centres focused on routine, replicable work face the greatest risk of restructuring, consolidation or closure.
Over the next 3–5 years, 30–40 per cent of smaller GCCs could successfully transform and remain captive, 20–30 per cent could become specialised centres, and 10–20 per cent could be carved out, acquired or transferred through build-operate-transfer models. The remainder could shrink materially or close.

indian-startups-2433238bae.fulltext:
[Text below is TechCrunch's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Cloud provider Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation, marking what could be its last private round before a planned 2027 IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. Coatue Management and Blackstone are leading the round.
A letter to investors reviewed by the Journal shows Lambda’s backlog grew from $15 billion in June to $50 billion in September. While that might look like a hearty increase in demand, much of that increase appears to be driven by a $35 billion commitment from one company: Anthropic, which signed a deal with Lambda in late August.
That means Lambda’s valuation, which has climbed significantly since its 2025 funding round, could be leaning heavily on Anthropic’s ability to keep paying. Still, with reliable GPU capacity so scarce, investors are clearly still willing to bet on companies that provide it, especially ones with large contracts with a major AI lab.
For neoclouds like Lambda, demand isn’t so much the problem as is the cost of meeting it. Data center buildouts are largely funded by debt — of which Lambda just raised an additional $1 billion last week — and lenders are getting choosier about who they offer cash to and under what circumstances. Lambda’s decision to raise more now not only sets the tone for its IPO pricing, but also gives it access to more capital before the scrutiny of public markets arrives.
If and when Lambda does IPO — the company was reportedly meant to debut this year, but has pushed that back amid market uncertainty — it will join other Nvidia-backed neoclouds, like CoreWeave and Nebius, that now depend on the health of their stock to fund their data center buildouts. British neocloud Nscale filed for an IPO last month and is expected to begin trading soon.
Lambda, Coatue, and Blackstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

global-economics-3e159fb445.headline: McDonald’s sued for allegedly using AI tool to determine pricing for franchises
global-economics-3e159fb445.fulltext:
McDonald’s is facing a lawsuit in federal court over its alleged use of an AI tool to determine pricing across independent franchises, which prosecutors say violates antitrust laws and has unfairly inflated menu prices for Americans.
The vast majority of McDonald’s US stores are independently owned and are said to individually decide on prices under company policy. Antitrust laws require businesses to set prices independently from their competitors, as coordinating prices can stifle market competition and push up costs for consumers.
The lawsuit, filed on 2 October in a federal Chicago courtroom, alleges that McDonald’s AI tool is illegal because it amounts to independent franchise locations exchanging nonpublic price and sales data.
“This case is about McDonald’s bringing ‘optimization’ to America’s largest fast food chain,” the complaint says. “McDonald’s has built and for years deployed its own information-sharing pricing platform, which draws on data from its millions of daily transactions to set menu prices across thousands of US restaurants. The result is algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin.”
In response to the lawsuit, a spokesperson for the McDonald’s corporation said that the “complaint is filled with inaccuracies and we will vigorously defend against this lawsuit”.
“AI does not set menu prices at McDonald’s restaurants – McDonald’s franchisees do,” it said. “Optional tools are available to franchisees to help them make the best decisions for their businesses and customers, but these tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way.”
A recent Reuters investigation reported that some McDonald’s franchise owners have been pressured by the company to use the AI pricing tools and record their deviations from the tool’s recommendations. McDonald’s contested that characterization, calling the Reuters reporting “speculative and uninformed”.
The litigation, which has been proposed as a nationwide class-action lawsuit, was first brought forward by an Illinois man named Michael Thomas. Thomas, a McDonald’s regular who is described as “price conscious”, found that the cost of his usual order – a Quarter Pounder with cheese, fries and a Coke – varied even within his neighborhood in DeKalb, Illinois. The attorney listed as representing Thomas did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Thomas does not appear to be alone in his experience. At a McDonald’s in Manhattan’s financial district, Chukwama Okeke, 43, was finishing a mango-pineapple smoothie that he bought as part of a value meal that cost about $15 – something he only gets about once a month.
Okeke said that when he orders the same meal at a McDonald’s in Brooklyn’s Crown Heights neighborhood, he ends up paying closer to $9.
“McDonald’s in Manhattan is much more expensive than those in Brooklyn,” he said. “I’ve notice in some areas if they have a lot of like foot traffic, the prices tend to get higher.”
Beatriz Milander, 27, who ordered a snack wrap, a small fries and an iced coffee for $11.51, hadn’t noticed a huge difference between what she pays in the financial district and what she pays in her Bronx neighborhood, but said prices overall had inched up.
“In the last few months, I’ve seen them do more deals or like lower-priced things,” she said. “But it definitely was pricing up for a little bit there.”
Experts say that companies using AI to set or alter pricing could exacerbate the country’s affordability crisis and make it harder for Americans to bear everyday costs. So far this year, at least 90 pieces of legislation have been filed across the country to push back against algorithmic price-fixing, according to Lindsay Owens, the head of the left-leaning thinktank Groundwork Collaborative, who recently authored a book on the topic.
McDonald’s acquired an AI company, Dynamic Yield, in 2019, but has firmly denied using AI in setting menu prices. In a statement released on 1 October, the day before the lawsuit was filed, the chain denied using dynamic pricing and described its pricing tool as simply providing information that franchises are free to decide whether to adopt.
The fast-food chain has been scrutinized over recent years for its elevated prices, and went viral in 2023 over an $18 Big Mac meal at a Connecticut McDonald’s. The franchise’s owner filed a lawsuit alleging that it was the AI pricing tool that suggested the $18 price to the franchise.
According to a fact sheet the chain published in 2024, the average price of a McDonald’s menu item increased about 40% between 2019 and 2024.

health-tech-d7198b4766.headline: Zuckerberg's Biohub expands virtual cell effort to $1.8B, with Meta, Google
health-tech-d7198b4766.fulltext:

Biohub announced on Wednesday that the U.S. government, Google parent Alphabet, and Meta are joining its Virtual Biology Initiative, bringing total commitments to $1.8 billion in funding, data, computation, and measurement technology to build open datasets for training AI models in biological research.
Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta have together committed $300 million to the initiative. Through a cross-agency effort called the Genesis Mission, the Department of Energy is directing more than $500 million across five years to support lab measurement, computational work, and modeling. NIH will help organize datasets and repositories that were assembled using more than $500 million in prior federal funding, with Biohub standardizing that material for use in AI model training.
Those commitments build on the $500 million pledged to the project in April by Biohub — founded as a philanthropic effort by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan — according to Reuters. The initiative's goal is to measure how cells respond to changes across a broader range of conditions than scientists have studied to date, then use that data to build predictive models capable of compressing drug development timelines.
"An accurate predictive model of biology could dramatically accelerate scientific discovery by enabling scientists to perform experiments digitally," Biohub Head of Science Alex Rives said in a statement.
The datasets will be released publicly, but companies that fund the work receive a period of exclusive access before that happens, Rives told Reuters. Government-funded work running in parallel will carry no such restrictions, he said.
Today's cell datasets top out in the hundreds of millions, Rives told Reuters, but he said a truly accurate predictive model would need data at the scale of billions — and ultimately trillions — of cells. Rives said the partners are targeting a five-year window for work that would otherwise stretch across decades, with an initial dataset slated to arrive in roughly a year and functional predictive models expected to follow within the same five-year horizon.
The initiative is drawing support beyond its primary funders. The Allen Institute, Broad Institute, Gladstone Institutes, the Human Cell Atlas, the Human Protein Atlas, and the Wellcome Sanger Institute have committed to working within the effort. NVIDIA will contribute computing infrastructure and technical expertise, and Renaissance Philanthropy is helping expand funding for data generation, Biohub said.
"Generating the data to solve predictive systems biology requires scaling past the limits of what any single organization can produce today," Isomorphic Labs President Max Jaderberg said in a statement.

climate-energy-d6f23504d2.headline: India’s EV retail sales jump 74% to record 3.33 lakh units in September: FADA
climate-energy-d6f23504d2.fulltext:
Written By  Ankit Kumar
Published: 6:00 PM, Oct 7, 2026 | Updated: 6:00 PM, Oct 7, 2026
India’s EV retail sales rose 74% year-on-year to a record 3.33 lakh units in September, with electric two-wheelers and passenger vehicles driving growth.
India’s EV retail sales jump 74% to record 3.33 lakh units in September: FADA
India’s electric vehicle (EV) retail sales reached a record high in September, with total registrations rising 74 per cent year-on-year (YoY) to 3,33,634 units, according to data released by the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) on Wednesday.
EV penetration across vehicle categories also increased to around 13 per cent in September, compared with approximately 10 per cent in the same month last year.
The record performance was driven by strong demand across mass-market segments, particularly electric two-wheelers and passenger vehicles, both of which recorded their highest-ever monthly retail sales.
FADA President Sai Giridhar said the September performance marked a significant milestone for India’s electric vehicle market.
Unlike the broader automobile market, where September growth was supported by a weak year-ago base, the EV segment recorded an absolute monthly sales record, Giridhar said.
“Festive demand, maturing running-cost economics, a widening choice of models and sustained policy support through PM E-DRIVE and progressive state schemes are together turning the EV from an alternative into a default consideration for a growing set of buyers,” he said.
Giridhar further said the growth was no longer primarily driven by subsidies, but by rising consumer demand.
“Electric mobility is now a durable thread of the India Growth Story and September shows it accelerating, not plateauing,” he said.
Electric two-wheeler (E2W) retail sales surged to an all-time high of 2,07,314 units in September, registering an 88.67 per cent YoY increase.
Sales also rose 13.16 per cent month-on-month (MoM). EV penetration in the two-wheeler segment increased to 11.6 per cent from 8.2 per cent a year earlier.
The segment accounted for the largest share of overall EV retail sales during the month.
Electric passenger vehicle (EPV) retail sales also reached a new monthly high of 36,108 units in September.
Sales increased 94.56 per cent YoY and 17.63 per cent MoM, while EV penetration in the passenger vehicle category rose to 8.5 per cent from 5.7 per cent in September last year.
The segment's record sales contributed significantly to the overall increase in EV retail volumes during the month.
Electric three-wheeler (E3W) retail sales stood at 86,024 units in September, registering 40 per cent YoY growth and 7.74 per cent MoM growth.
EV penetration in the three-wheeler segment remained particularly strong at 64.9 per cent.
The category continued to record the highest EV penetration among the vehicle segments covered in the FADA data.
Electric commercial vehicle (ECV) retail sales stood at 4,188 units during the month.
Although sales declined 10.9 per cent MoM, the segment recorded strong YoY growth of 158 per cent.
EV penetration in the commercial vehicle category improved to around 4 per cent in September, compared with 2.16 per cent a year earlier.
The September data highlights the broad-based expansion of electric mobility across India's automobile market, with electric two-wheelers and passenger vehicles setting new monthly sales records.

Bloomberg's Mike McKee said that the Fed's decision to raise rates was unanimous among all nineteen members of the FOMC, including non-voting participants, according to minutes from the Fed's September meeting. McKee said the minutes showed that members feel that between inflation numbers, the geopolitical situation and AI buildout they are not making enough progress on inflation
Let's toss to Michael McKee. He is outside the Federal Reserve.
Well, guys, the decision to raise interest rates at the September meeting was unanimous, not just among the voting members of the Open market Committee, but all 19 members of the Open market Committee supported the rate move, the minute show. Inflation remained elevated and risks were tilted to the upside, while the labor market appeared to be near full employment. Quote, based on the outlook and the changing balance of risks, all participants viewed a higher target range for the federal funds rate as appropriate. Goes on to say, many participants emphasized that a higher rate path would be prudent on risk management grounds, while a number of participants viewed a higher path as necessary based on their modal outlooks rather than on risk management grounds. Some saw raising rates as a way to prevent inflation expectations from becoming unanchored, while others felt it would keep inflation from broadening out. Many also noted that financial conditions appeared to be supportive of economic growth and several noted that they viewed the current policy rate as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive, which leads us to the important quote. With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target rate for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end. Along with a firming labor market, participants saw the economy expanding at a solid pace, driven by robust business investment and by resilient consumer spending. One negative, agriculture, strained because of worsening drought and higher prices for diesel and other inputs, the minutes say. The K-shaped economy came in for a mention. Some participants observed the strong demand for skilled workers in sectors related to the ongoing AI buildout had been driving strong wage gains, but aggregate wage growth was moderate and not a source of inflationary pressure. So, while all of this was three weeks ago, it underscores that recent comments by senior Open Market Committee officials about not moving October 28th does not mean they will not move before the end of the year. Going into the next set of meetings, it looks like they've got one more at least on the books.
Ah, and this is what investors were looking for. Mike, you're going to stay with us. I just want to do a quick check on the markets. Uh not seeing much movement, maybe a little bit of a tilt to the downside, but not really. S&P was down about 19, that's where it is right now. Uh Nasdaq 100 was down about 116 points before the Fed minutes. It's still just down about 113. More importantly, we got to look at the yield curve. Uh in terms of what we've seen in treasuries and throughout the morning we've seen them back off their highs. Um the 10-year note, which was at about 528, that's exactly where we find it. Uh same story for the two, no changes there. Uh same story uh for the five years. So, Mike, bah humbug, not interesting. I don't know what we say. Um, we thought this was going to be kind of stale because of some of the new data that we've gotten since. But is, it does sound like it's pretty important that we now have an indication from the Fed that they are thinking we need one more rate increase.
Definitely, that comes out in the minutes and the idea that all of the participants, all 19 of them agreed with the rate hike and that means even uh people who might have been dovish but not voting suggests that they do see uh as a unit the need for higher rates and they did see essentially a need for higher rates by the end of the year. Now, uh we have heard from John Williams and Philip Jefferson in recent days suggesting maybe not at the October meeting. A lot of that will depend on what happens uh next Wednesday when we get the CPI report. But uh it does look like that unless there's some surprise downward move in inflation, that they are teeing up right now for a December 9th move.
Hey Mike, question for you. So is the the dominant explanation for the higher rates, is that still inflation or or is has it shifted a bit more to to labor market data?
Oh, it's definitely inflation. Labor market data they noted with wages uh not moving up very much in the aggregate, it doesn't produce any wage pressures. But the inflation numbers, the geopolitical situation, uh what's happening with the AI buildout and the fact that that's pushing up prices, and also some of them noting that service industry prices were still elevated. All of that together uh suggests that they are not making enough progress on inflation. It comes down to what do they think the neutral rate is and they all in their uh SEP said they thought that the neutral rate had moved up and that requires higher interest rates. So, uh they're comfortable with where they are now, but think that they might need to do more in order to keep uh inflation on a downward path.
Hey, Mike, um Chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters following that September 16th decision that the move was aimed at removing quote dose of accommodation as inflation remained stubbornly high. His comments fueled market pets at the time for another increase in in October, but we have two more meetings. Um, is it safe to say Kevin Warsh is truly looking at the data and there's nothing political here based on what we maybe are gleaning from some of the minutes?
Oh, absolutely. It looks like Kevin Warsh is going back to his, uh, shall we say, old normal self, uh, to steal Mohamed El-Erian's line. Uh, he has always been a hawk and he sees the inflation problem now as uh needing higher rates. It's what he said at the news conference. We haven't heard from him lately, but he is speaking next week, so we may get a reaffirmation of that. I don't think, and I have talked to several Fed officials in recent days, who vociferously argue that the election doesn't play a role, but it would be easier for them not to raise rates right before the election if they can avoid it and they don't have to get caught up in all the politics about it. So if we get a reasonable CPI and PPI report next week, then they can follow through with the idea that they're not going to move at this meeting, but they still see inflation pressures strong enough that they need to raise rates one more time and they did emphasize by the end of the year.
Hey Mike, you just mentioned you are talking to Fed officials. You're always talking to Fed officials. You sit in the row right behind me and I know you're always in touch and you're working on things for Wall Street week and and other parts of the Bloomberg universe. But I I am curious, um, does it feel like Fed officials are much more optimistic about the outlook in terms of growth and not worrying about the rate increases slowing down growth or creating problems when it comes to equity valuations or other parts of the market. I mean, you know, higher rates can certainly, it takes a while for them to be felt through, but it can create certainly some slowdowns longer term.
Well, they are looking six months, eight months, 12 months out in terms of when their rate moves will hit the economy, but they don't seem to be worried about it having an impact on the stock market right now or on economic activity. They note in the minutes that credit remains widely available, that spreads remain relatively tight, and even with the AI buildout, uh there doesn't seem to be a problem with people getting loans. So they don't seem to be having an impact overall on the outlook for continued growth. Now, the question is how high would they have to go to have some sort of impact? And what kind of impact are they looking for? Because normally you raise rates to crimp demand and demand falls, employers let workers go and the economy slows down. Right now, we're seeing uh what some Fed officials have described to me as incrementally increased demand for workers, a lot of that in the AI sector and they're not seeing any real slowdown in business activity. Business investment remains strong. So do they really have to push it farther? That's something they're going to be watching as the inflation numbers come out.

Sunfox Technologies, the Dehradun-based medtech company behind the Spandan portable ECG platform, has raised $7 million (approx. Rs 67 crore) in a Series A funding round co-led by Ashish Kacholia, Lashit Sanghvi, Alchemy Capital and 3one4 Capital.
The startup had previously raised Rs 15 crore in a pre-Series A funding round led by Venture Catalysts, with participation from Finvolve through the IA Growth Opportunities Fund I and Brew Opportunities Fund, Universal Group, RP Singhvi Group and others in August 2024. It also secured investments from all five Sharks in the first season of Shark Tank India.
The fresh funds will be used for the next phase of growth, including expanding its presence across India, developing global go-to-market capabilities, scaling the organisation and continuing investments in research and development, Sunfox said in a press release.
Founded in 2016 by Rajat Jain, Arpit Jain, Saurabh Badola, Nitin Chandola and Sabit Rawat, Sunfox Technologies develops portable and AI-enabled healthcare solutions, with a focus on diagnostic access, particularly in cardiac care.
Its flagship Spandan series is a portable, medical-grade ECG platform designed for use across hospitals, clinics, telemedicine networks and home-based patient monitoring. The platform enables ECGs to be recorded closer to patients and can flag cardiac patterns that may require further medical attention.
Over the past decade, Sunfox has developed a range of Spandan ECG solutions for personal, clinical and institutional use, with applications across home-based ECG recording, clinics, hospitals, public-health programmes and remote-care networks.
Sunfox said it has expanded its presence to more than 15 countries, while its products have reached healthcare providers across more than 1,800 PIN codes in India. Its technology can also be deployed through a hub-and-spoke model in public-health systems.
The company said around 60,000 Spandan devices have been deployed across India, covering more than 20,000 villages across states and union territories. Its Spandan One platform has been used to screen approximately 5 million patients annually.
Sunfox competes with players such as AliveCor and Tricog in the cardiac monitoring and diagnostics space.
Meanwhile, Monitra Health has raised fresh capital this year for its remote cardiac monitoring platform. Beyond cardiac care, companies such as Molbio Diagnostics are expanding portable point-of-care diagnostics through its battery-operated Truenat platform.

Software startup Vinci said on Tuesday it raised $250 million at a $1.5 billion valuation and is seeking to expand its suite of software used to simulate elements of chip and other hardware design.
The Palo Alto, California-based company is entering a market that includes similar AI-based simulation products from established chip design software firms such as Cadence and Synopsys.
Vinci's software is capable of high-fidelity physics simulation that is useful for chip and hardware designers - AI chips generate enormous amounts of heat - as the systems get larger and more complex. The company began by focusing on thermal simulation for chips but is looking to expand to help simulate whole systems.
"If you ask anybody, what they are interested in - they want higher and higher fidelity physics simulation," Vinci CEO Hardik Kabaria said in an interview.
The 70-person startup plans to use the proceeds from the funding round to pay for its computing costs, hire more staff and continue expanding its range of simulation products. Eventually Vinci plans to expand to other types of physics simulation like vibration testing and electromagnetics.
"It is a foundation model that is proven to work in the field, so now it's about scaling up the operations and that means not just two pilot deployments but 20," Kabaria said, referring to the foundation AI model the company built to assist with the simulations.
Advent, Temasek and Xora Innovation led the funding round. Venture firms Eclipse, Khosla Ventures and Madrona also participated, the company said.

The Palo Alto, California-based company is entering a market that includes similar AI-based simulation products from established chip design software firms such as Cadence and Synopsys.
